crime.value: Rape-murder of a teenage girl in City Park, bludgeoned with a rock; the boyfriend reports she was kidnapped by three men — central question: is his abduction story true?
crime.quote: "Three men!" the boy panted. "They kidnapped my girl."

victim.value: Helen MacKenzie, teenage girl from Wells Street, of lower social class than her wealthy boyfriend; killed when she resisted his sexual advances
victim.quote: The young girl lay dead and cold under a tree. Her pants were down, her skirt was up...

closed_world.value: City Park at night by the pond and adjoining woods, isolated with only the couple present; broadened only by the reported car of yelling boys
closed_world.quote: When they drove past the pond, Wainwright pointed to a stand of trees, black against the moonlit sky.

culprit_and_motive.value: Lawrence Wainwright, the boyfriend — he struck her with a rock to subdue her when she resisted sex, killed her accidentally, then invented the kidnappers
culprit_and_motive.quote: you were determined and you hit her with a rock to quiet her down, only... you'd hit her too hard and she was dead

resolution.value: Galton reasons from behavioral logic — three attackers would need no rock and would not have killed her while leaving him alive — confronts the boy, who breaks down sobbing; physical evidence on the body promised
resolution.quote: "But three men? What would they need a rock for? Two could hold her for the third so tight she couldn't move a muscle."

investigator.value: Captain Mike Galton, veteran police captain of detectives relying on experience with human nature, with young sidekick Detective Bill Dennis
investigator.quote: "Human nature," said Mike Gallon, the captain of detectives, "is the key to man's universe."

suspect_architecture.value: Effectively one real suspect — Lawrence Wainwright, the boyfriend who reports the crime — set against three phantom 'abductors' (two dark, one blond) he invents. The yelling boys in the cream convertible, corroborated by an independent complaint call, serve as the only alternative candidates; they have apparent opportunity but no proven existence at the scene.
suspect_architecture.quote: “Three men!” the boy panted. “They kidnapped my girl.”

red_herring.value: The cream-colored convertible with three rowdy boys, independently reported to police at 9:42 by Mrs. Stanley Turner — a real nuisance call the killer opportunistically grafts his false story onto, giving it apparent corroboration.
red_herring.quote: Call from a Mrs. Stanley Turner on Westlake Avenue about a light-colored convertible with three boys in it

clue_fairness.value: Fair: all data the reader needs is on the page before Galton's deduction — the boy's own account of three assailants, the rock used to subdue the girl, his survival with only superficial injuries, the girl's stripped body, and his reluctance to give names/addresses before rushing police to the park.
clue_fairness.quote: a red-stained rock, wrenched from the nearby earth, lay beside her.

social_world.value: Small-city class divide: Wainwright is a nineteen-year-old from 'one of the best sections of town' with a shiny new hardtop; Helen MacKenzie lives on Wells Street, a lower social station — the detectives immediately read the cross-class date as sexual exploitation. Set against the police-station hierarchy of veteran captain, young sidekick, and desk sergeant.
social_world.quote: She comes from a different social station than you do... usually when men date girls below their social class, it’s for only one reason.

alibi.value: No conventional alibi; the suspect instead places himself at the scene as a victim, claiming he was knocked unconscious during the abduction (~10:45) and thus absent in mind if not body — an 'unconsciousness alibi' that also explains his injuries and dishevelment.
alibi.quote: “I tried to fight them, but they ganged up and knocked me out. And when I came to, they were gone and she was gone.”

reveal_mechanic.value: Psychological/logical demonstration from criminal behavior patterns: Galton reasons that three attackers who wanted rape would have no need of a rock (two could hold her) and no motive to kill her, while a lone assailant would — so the story's internal logic, not physical evidence, convicts. Sealed by the threat of forensic examination of the body, which breaks the boy into sobs.
reveal_mechanic.quote: “But three men? What would they need a rock for? Two could hold her for the third so tight she couldn’t move a muscle.”

media_and_audience.value: No press; the 'audience' is the police institution itself — the blotter, radio dispatch, and the ring of thirty encircling officers whose cold, disbelieving faces form the jury before which the boy's story collapses.
media_and_audience.quote: He looked around desperately, but all the faces were cold and disbelieving.

investigator_wound.value: Galton's professional creed — that an experienced cop knows human nature better than any psychiatrist — is the vulnerability the case tests; he 'smelled' the lie immediately yet hoped against his own judgment that the boy was telling the truth, and is wearied and saddened when experience proves right.
investigator_wound.quote: “I hoped like hell you were telling the truth, but when she wasn’t in by midnight, I was afraid you weren’t.”

victims_enemies.value: Helen MacKenzie has no enemies in any conventional sense; her only antagonist is her own boyfriend, Lawrence Wainwright, a wealthy boy dating a girl from Wells Street — 'a different social station' — whose relationship is defined by class asymmetry and sexual pressure rather than grievance.
victims_enemies.quote: She comes from a different social station than you do... usually when men date girls below their social class, it's for only one reason.

suspect_wounds.value: Wainwright's vulnerability is his need to appear respectable: the good address, the shiny new hardtop, the insistence that he isn't a snob and that they'd 'talked about marriage.' The crime activates his terror of being seen as a boy who took a lower-class girl into the park for one reason, and his lies escalate to protect that self-image.
suspect_wounds.quote: Wainwright said heatedly, "I'm not a snob. We happen to like each other. We've talked about marriage, if you really want to know."

unreliable_frame.value: The entire narrative is filtered through Wainwright's report to the police — the only account of the attack, delivered by the killer himself. His story shifts under questioning (from 'kissing' to 'necking' to 'we also talk'), and Galton reads him as a liar from the moment he bursts in.
unreliable_frame.quote: "I've heard so many phonies I could smell this one the moment you came in tonight."

setting_as_constraint.value: City Park at night under a full moon — a known lovers' lane where 'neckers' are raided — supplies both the isolation for the crime and the ready-made alibi. The genuine complaint about a cream-colored convertible full of yelling boys, logged at 9:42 by the desk sergeant, gave Wainwright a real, police-corroborated set of phantom attackers to blame.
setting_as_constraint.quote: "If a bunch of boys want to raid neckers, Cap, this is the night to find them."

evidence_type.value: Primarily testimonial/behavioral logic — Galton's deduction from the internal inconsistency of the story (a live boy and a dead girl are incompatible with three attackers). Backed by the threat of forensic evidence: the body's forthcoming examination, which triggers the confession.
evidence_type.quote: "That girl's body is going to be examined very, very carefully for physical evidence."

false_suspect.value: The three boys in the cream-colored convertible — real hell-raisers whose 9:42 p.m. noise complaint makes them plausible abductors, invoked by Wainwright to divert the search into the woods and away from himself.
false_suspect.quote: "this cream-colored convertible went racing past us with three boys in it yelling and screaming. I think they were the same ones."

technical_detail.value: Galton's expertise is applied criminal psychology of group sexual assault: three men would have no need of a rock, since two could hold a victim for the third; and a gang bent on rape would beat the boyfriend but leave the girl alive. The rock and the surviving male witness together are physically incompatible with the claimed scenario.
technical_detail.quote: "One man, maybe. You, alone, might have to use a rock to have your way with her. But three men? What would they need a rock for?"

moral_ambiguity.value: Wainwright is not a predator by design but a nineteen-year-old whose sexual insistence turned lethal by accident — he hit her 'to quiet her down' and found he'd hit too hard. His grief and shock appear genuine; his lie is panic, not calculation, and the story ends with him sobbing rather than condemned.
moral_ambiguity.quote: you hit her with a rock to quiet her down, only, when it was all over, you found out you'd hit her too hard and she was dead.
